doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: Houston sessions, St. Thomas High and Harry Lantz's youth orchestra
summary: Houston drummers and clubs, his parochial high school and the youth orchestra under Harry Lantz.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: with a lot of good drummers: Malcolm Pinson; a great drummer named Carl Lott who’s still alive, a great drummer; Richie Lockwood, I don’t know what happened to Richie. But man, and there were at least four or five full time jazz clubs in Houston back then.
Did you get a reputation in your high school like you’re a cool cat, man?

No. Not really. I led a double life. I went to a very good parochial high school, St. Thomas High School. And my father sent me there because he had gone to a parochial high school in Tulsa when he was a kid. He said later with the public schools if you go to St. Thomas you’re really going to get an education, and I did. It was harder than university in some ways. So they had no music program really. They did but it was in its early stages and it really wasn’t happening. So what I was mainly involved in were my sessions and then I played in an incredible youth orchestra. That’s where I got the timpani thing happening, led by a man named Harry Lantz, one of the greatest educators ever, ever, ever, ever. L-A-N-T-Z. Harry Lantz. And this orchestra was so good that Leopold Stokowski, who at the time was conducting the Houston Symphony, would come over and just rehearse us for the fun of it. I mean it was that good. It was an incredible youth orchestra. Sir Malcolm Sargent, when he was in town, came over. So — and so that was a really — that experience, playing under Harry Lantz in that youth orchestra was just as important from the standpoint of discipline and focus, concentration, responsibility, as were those jazz gigs I was playing. So I had it good on both ends. It was just a remarkable situation when I go back and think about it. But like a lot of things, you don’t fully appreciate it ‘til you’re old enough to understand it.
